structured.lead: Identify the work below that does not belong to the literature of the eighteenth century
structured.options_hint: Advancement of Learning Gulliver's Trave

items.explanation: Francis Bacon's The Advancement of Learning was published in 1605 during the Jacobean era (early seventeenth century). By contrast, The Spectator (1711–12), Gulliver's Travels (1726), and Alexander Pope's Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot (1735) are all major works of eighteenth-century Augustan literature.

structured.lead:
Which, among the following, is a place through which John Bunyan's
Christian does NOT pass ?
structured.options_hint: The Slough of Despond Mount Helicon The

items.explanation: In John Bunyan's Christian allegory The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), Christian journeys through the Slough of Despond, the Valley of Humiliation, and Vanity Fair on his way to the Celestial City. Mount Helicon is a mountain from classical Greek mythology sacred to the Muses, not a place in Bunyan's work.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2012 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem:

about The Lyrical Ballads is NOT
true ?

structured.lead: Which of the following statements about The Lyrical Ballads is NOT true ?
structured.options_hint: It carried only one ballad proper, which

options: It carried only one ballad proper, which was Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
It also carried pastoral and other poems
It carried a "Preface" which Wordsworth added in 1800
It also printed from Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
items.explanation: Lyrical Ballads (1798), co-authored by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, contained original Romantic poems and did not reprint Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751). In his 1800 'Preface', Wordsworth only quoted a sonnet by Gray to critique artificial poetic diction.

structured.options_hint: William Golding, The Inheritors Philip L

items.explanation: Samuel Beckett's play Waiting for Godot was first published in French in 1952 (premiered in 1953) and in English translation in 1954. William Golding's The Inheritors, Philip Larkin's The Less Deceived, and the British edition of William Empson's Collected Poems were all published in 1955.

"weak" and popularized the practice of misreading
structured.options_hint: Alan Bloom Harold Bloom Geoffrey Hartman

items.explanation: In The Anxiety of Influence (1973) and A Map of Misreading (1975), American critic Harold Bloom argued that 'strong' poets overcome the stifling influence of their great predecessors through creative 'misreading' (misprision), whereas 'weak' poets merely imitate them.

items.explanation: Throughout Alexander Pope's mock-heroic poem The Rape of the Lock (1712/1714), Belinda's radiant beauty and bright eyes are repeatedly compared to the sun, which they rival and eclipse from the moment she wakes.

items.explanation: At the time of this 2012 examination, the Jnanpith (Gyanpeeth) Award was restricted to Indian languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, excluding English (until Amitav Ghosh became the first English-language recipient in 2018). Gorboduc is a tragedy, while Ralph Roister Doister and Gammer Gurton's Needle are comedies

items.explanation: Gorboduc (1561), written by Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville, is the first English blank-verse tragedy, whereas Nicholas Udall's Ralph Roister Doister (c. 1552) and Gammer Gurton's Needle (c. 1553) are the earliest sixteenth-century English comedies.

structured.lead: W.M. Thackeray's Vanity Fair owes its title to

items.explanation: William Makepeace Thackeray took the title of his satirical novel Vanity Fair (1847–48) from John Bunyan's allegory The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), where 'Vanity Fair' is a never-ending fair in the town of Vanity symbolizing worldly attachment to sin and materialism.

items.explanation: Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837–1909) was a late Victorian poet, whereas Robert Southey (1774–1843), Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832), and William Hazlitt (1778–1830) were direct Romantic-era contemporaries of William Wordsworth (1770–1850) and S. T. Coleridge (1772–1834).

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2012 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The term invective refers to

structured.lead: The term invective refers to
structured.options_hint: the abusive writing or speech in which t

options: the abusive writing or speech in which there is harsh denunciation of some person or thing
an insulting writing attack upon a real person, in verse or prose, usually involving caricature and ridicule
a written or spoken text in which an apparently straightforward statement or event is undermined in its context so as to give it a very different significance
the chanting or reciting of words deemed to have magical power
items.explanation: In literary terminology, invective refers to direct, harsh denunciation of a person or thing through abusive speech or writing. By contrast, an attack using caricature and ridicule is a lampoon, undermining a straightforward statement is irony, and chanting magical words is an incantation.

structured.lead: The Enlightenment was characterized by
structured.options_hint: accelerated industrial production and ge

options: accelerated industrial production and general well- being of the public
a belief in the universal authority of reason and emphasis on scientific experimentation
Protestant work ethic and compliance with Christian values of life
an undue faith in predestination and neglect of free will
items.explanation: The Enlightenment (or Age of Reason) of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was defined by a belief in the universal authority of human reason, empirical scientific inquiry, and skepticism toward traditional dogma.

structured.lead: Which Shakespearean play contains the line: "...there is a special providence in the fall of a sparrow" ?
structured.options_hint: King Lear Hamlet Coriolanus Macbeth

items.explanation: Prince Hamlet speaks this line to Horatio in Act V, Scene 2 of William Shakespeare's Hamlet just before his fatal fencing match with Laertes, expressing his philosophical acceptance of divine providence and fate ('The readiness is all').

items.stem: What does the term episteme signify ?

structured.lead: What does the term episteme signify ?
structured.options_hint: Knowledge Archive Theology Scholarship

items.explanation: Derived from the ancient Greek word epistēmē meaning 'knowledge' or 'science', the term was popularized in critical theory by Michel Foucault in The Order of Things (1966) to signify the underlying historical framework of knowledge in a particular era.

items.explanation: Echoing Sir Philip Sidney's classic definition of poetry in An Apology for Poetry (1595) as 'a speaking picture—with this end, to teach and delight', a literary image is best defined as a vivid verbal 'speaking picture'.

structured.lead: Whom did Keats regard as the prime example of 'negative capability' ?
structured.options_hint: John Milton William Wordsworth William S

items.explanation: In a December 1817 letter to his brothers George and Tom, John Keats defined 'Negative Capability'—the ability to remain in uncertainties, mysteries, and doubts without irritable reaching after fact and reason—and cited William Shakespeare as its supreme exemplar.

items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence of publication is Oliver Goldsmith's 'The Deserted Village' (1770), William Blake's 'A Poison Tree' (1794), Percy Bysshe Shelley's 'Ozymandias' (1818), and Dante Gabriel Rossetti's 'The Blessed Damozel' (1850).

I. a quatrain, unrhymed, but alliterative
II. a stanza of four lines in iambic pentameter
III. an eight-line stanza in iambic pentameter followed by a ninth in six iambic feet
IV. an eight-line stanza with six iambic feet followed by a ninth in iambic pentameter
structured.options_hint: I and II II III IV

items.explanation: Invented by Edmund Spenser for The Faerie Queene (1590–1596), the Spenserian stanza consists of eight lines in iambic pentameter followed by a ninth alexandrine line in iambic hexameter (six iambic feet), rhyming ababbcbcc (III).
